lead: This unit turns the first and second laws into working equations for real fluids. You learn how to get entropy, enthalpy and free-energy changes from pressure, volume, temperature and heat-capacity data, and how to read steam tables and charts. After it you can derive Maxwell relations, compute residual properties and use the Clausius-Clapeyron equation for saturation pressure.
about: This unit turns the first and second laws into working equations for property changes. It starts with the Helmholtz and Gibbs free energies and their equilibrium tests, writes the four fundamental property relations for U, H, A and G, and obtains the Maxwell relations from them. Residual properties then carry an equation of state into enthalpy, entropy and fugacity. Steam tables, quality and property diagrams handle two-phase systems, and the Clausius–Clapeyron equation gives the slope of a saturation curve. The last two chapters relate C<sub>P</sub>, C<sub>V</sub> and their ratio to PVT data and give the Jacobian method, a fixed recipe for any partial derivative.

chapters.idea: Helmholtz and Gibbs free energies are Legendre transforms that measure useful work at constant T,V and constant T,P.
chapters.depth: Define A = U − TS and G = H − TS = U + PV − TS. Give units J or J/mol. Write dA = −SdT − PdV and dG = −SdT + VdP. State equilibrium criteria dA ≤ 0 at constant T,V and dG ≤ 0 at constant T,P. Connect A to maximum work at constant T,V and G to maximum non-PV work at constant T,P. Some syllabi call A the Helmholtz free energy F. Mention the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation ∂(G/T)/∂T at constant P = −H/T² in one line.

figure.title: From U to A and G
figure.aria: U is transformed to A by subtracting TS and to H by adding PV; H is transformed to G by subtracting TS.

chapters.example: One mole of ideal gas at 300 K is compressed isothermally and reversibly from 1 bar to 5 bar. Calculate ΔA and ΔG. Answer: ΔA = ΔG = nRT ln(P2/P1) = 1 × 8.314 × 300 × ln(5/1) = 4.01 kJ.
chapters.trap: Using G = U − TS instead of G = H − TS; forgetting to use kelvin; losing the positive sign for compression.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 internal energy and enthalpy; Unit 3 entropy.
chapters.leave: PVT calculations and equations of state to Unit 2; fugacity and chemical potential to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: The four fundamental relations collect the first and second laws into exact differentials for U, H, A and G.
chapters.depth: Derive dU = TdS − PdV from a reversible closed simple compressible system. Obtain dH = TdS + VdP, dA = −SdT − PdV and dG = −SdT + VdP by Legendre transforms. Identify natural variables: (S,V) for U, (S,P) for H, (T,V) for A, (T,P) for G. Read coefficient identities such as (∂U/∂S)_V = T and (∂U/∂V)_S = −P. Some syllabi call these the thermodynamic property relations. Show how to integrate the relations for property changes.

figure.aria: U is the root; adding PV gives H, subtracting TS gives A, and subtracting TS from H gives G, with each potential showing its differential.

chapters.example: For a van der Waals gas P = RT/(V − b) − a/V² with a = 0.364 Pa m⁶ mol⁻² and V = 0.200 m³ mol⁻¹, calculate (∂U/∂V)_T. Use (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂P/∂T)_V − P. Answer: a/V² = 0.364/(0.200)² = 9.1 Pa.
chapters.trap: Mixing up natural variables; using the wrong sign for P dV; treating a partial derivative as a simple fraction.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 first law; Unit 2 equations of state; Unit 3 entropy.
chapters.leave: Maxwell relation applications to chapter 4.3; residual-property integrals to chapter 4.4.

chapters.idea: Maxwell relations come from equality of mixed second derivatives of the potentials and replace entropy derivatives by measurable P,V,T derivatives.
chapters.depth: Derive the four relations: (∂T/∂V)_S = −(∂P/∂S)_V, (∂T/∂P)_S = (∂V/∂S)_P, (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V and (∂S/∂P)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_P. Show how each comes from dU, dH, dA or dG. Apply them to entropy changes, to (∂H/∂P)_T = V − T(∂V/∂T)_P, and to the Joule-Thomson coefficient. Some syllabi write Maxwell's thermodynamic relations.

figure.title: Four differentials give four Maxwell relations
figure.aria: The four exact differentials dU, dH, dA and dG are connected by Legendre transforms; each gives one Maxwell relation by equal mixed second derivatives.

chapters.example: Use a Maxwell relation to calculate ΔS when 2 mol of ideal gas at 300 K is compressed from 1 bar to 10 bar. Answer: ΔS = −nR ln(P2/P1) = −2 × 8.314 × ln(10) = −38.3 J/K.
chapters.trap: Getting the sign wrong; holding the wrong variable constant; using Celsius instead of kelvin.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2; Unit 2 ideal gas; Unit 3 entropy.
chapters.leave: Residual-property formulas to chapter 4.4; fugacity relations to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A residual property is the difference between a real-fluid property and its ideal-gas value at the same temperature and pressure.
chapters.depth: Define M^R = M − M^ig at the same T and P. Explain M^ig for H and U depends only on T, while S^ig and G^ig depend on P. Give G^R/RT = ln φ = ∫0^P (Z − 1) dP/P, H^R = ∫0^P [V − T(∂V/∂T)_P] dP, S^R = ∫0^P [(∂V/∂T)_P − R/P] dP and V^R = (Z − 1)RT/P. Show how cubic equations of state and generalized correlations supply these values. Cross-reference fugacity coefficient to Unit 5.

figure.title: Residual property as a departure
figure.aria: The real-gas property and the ideal-gas property at the same temperature and pressure are compared; their difference is the residual property.

chapters.example: At 300 K and 50 bar, a gas has fugacity coefficient φ = 0.90. Calculate its residual Gibbs energy per mole. Answer: G^R = RT ln φ = 8.314 × 300 × ln(0.90) = −262.8 J/mol.
chapters.trap: Using the same T and V instead of the same T and P; forgetting that an ideal-gas residual property is zero; mishandling the sign of ln φ.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2; Unit 2 compressibility factor; Unit 5 fugacity coefficient.
chapters.leave: Fugacity and activity models to Unit 5; phase equilibrium calculations to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: In a two-phase region the property is the mass-weighted average of saturated liquid and saturated vapour values, using quality.
chapters.depth: Explain saturated liquid, saturated vapour, wet mixture and superheated vapour. Define quality x = m_g/(m_f + m_g). Use M = (1 − x)M_f + xM_g for v, u, h and s; write h = h_f + x h_fg and v = v_f + x(v_g − v_f). Show how to read steam tables and interpolate. Introduce P-v, T-s, h-s Mollier and P-h diagrams. Some syllabi call these thermodynamic property charts. Apply to steam power and refrigeration cycles by reference to Unit 3.

figure.title: Steam table excerpt at 10 bar
figure.aria: Three table rows show saturated liquid, wet mixture and saturated vapour, with quality used to interpolate between the saturated liquid and vapour columns.

chapters.example: Steam at 10 bar has quality 0.90. Given h_f = 762.8 kJ/kg, h_fg = 2015.3 kJ/kg, v_f = 0.001127 m³/kg and v_g = 0.1944 m³/kg, calculate h and v. Answer: h = 762.8 + 0.90 × 2015.3 = 2576.6 kJ/kg; v = 0.001127 + 0.90 × (0.1944 − 0.001127) = 0.1751 m³/kg.
chapters.trap: Using h_g instead of h_fg; treating quality as a volume fraction; interpolating in the wrong table region.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 enthalpy; Unit 2 phase diagrams; Unit 3 steam cycles.
chapters.leave: Phase-equilibrium theory to Unit 6; mixture properties to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation gives the slope of a saturation curve from latent heat and volume change.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this inside this unit. Derive dP_sat/dT = ΔH/(T ΔV). Apply the ideal-vapour approximation ΔV ≈ V_g and constant ΔH to get ln(P2/P1) = −(ΔH/R)(1/T2 − 1/T1). Show the straight-line plot of ln P against 1/T. Use it to estimate vapour pressure and latent heat. Some syllabi write Clausius–Clapeyron.

figure.aria: A straight line of ln P against 1/T has slope −ΔH/R and shows how saturation pressure falls as temperature falls.

chapters.example: Water has ΔH_vap = 40.65 kJ/mol and normal boiling point 373 K at 1 atm. Estimate its saturation pressure at 350 K. Answer: ln(P2/P1) = −(40650/8.314)(1/350 − 1/373) = −0.8613, so P2 = 101.325 × e^−0.8613 = 42.8 kPa ≈ 0.423 bar.
chapters.trap: Putting T in degrees Celsius; dropping the negative sign; using liquid volume instead of the volume change.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.5; Unit 2 phase diagrams; Unit 3 latent heat.
chapters.leave: Full phase-equilibrium calculations to Unit 6; fugacity-based VLE to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Cp − Cv, the heat-capacity ratio and pressure or volume dependence of heat capacities follow from PVT derivatives.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this inside this unit. Give Cp − Cv = T v α²/κ_T = −T(∂P/∂T)_V²/(∂P/∂V)_T, where α = (1/v)(∂v/∂T)_P and κ_T = −(1/v)(∂v/∂P)_T. Define γ = Cp/Cv. State (∂Cp/∂P)_T = −T(∂²V/∂T²)_P and (∂Cv/∂V)_T = T(∂²P/∂T²)_V. Show Cp − Cv = R for an ideal gas. Mention the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation as a related free-energy relation.

figure.title: Cp − Cv from PVT data
figure.aria: Temperature and molar volume combine with thermal expansion coefficient and isothermal compressibility to give Cp − Cv.

chapters.example: For liquid water at 300 K, α = 2.57 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, κ_T = 4.50 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹ and v = 18.0 × 10⁻⁶ m³/mol. Calculate Cp − Cv. Answer: Cp − Cv = T v α²/κ_T = 300 × 18.0 × 10⁻⁶ × (2.57 × 10⁻⁴)²/(4.50 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 0.793 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
chapters.trap: Using Cp − Cv = R for a liquid; mixing mass and molar volume; getting the sign of α or κ_T wrong.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.3; Unit 1 heat capacities; Unit 2 PVT behaviour.
chapters.leave: Heat-capacity data for mixtures to Unit 5; reaction heat effects to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: The Jacobian method is a systematic calculus tool for transforming any thermodynamic partial derivative into measurable P,V,T and heat-capacity terms.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this inside this unit. Review the chain rule and the cyclic relation (∂x/∂y)_z(∂y/∂z)_x(∂z/∂x)_y = −1. Define the Jacobian J(u,v) = ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y). Show identities such as (∂u/∂x)_y = J(u,y)/J(x,y). Treat Maxwell relations as Jacobian ratios. Use the method to derive (∂H/∂P)_T and entropy derivatives.

figure.title: Jacobian transformation
figure.aria: A target derivative is rewritten as a Jacobian ratio, expanded into pressure-volume-temperature derivatives, and evaluated as a measurable result.

chapters.example: Use the Jacobian method to show (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V for an ideal gas, then evaluate it at 300 K and v = 0.0240 m³/mol. Answer: (∂P/∂T)_V = R/v = 8.314/0.0240 = 346 Pa/K = 346 J m⁻³ K⁻¹.
chapters.trap: Treating differentials as fractions; reversing the Jacobian orientation; losing the sign from the cyclic relation.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.2 and 4.3; Unit 2 ideal gas; Unit 3 entropy.
chapters.leave: Fugacity and chemical potential to Unit 5; phase equilibrium to Unit 6; reaction equilibrium to Unit 7.
